utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I would just like to inquire into a submission made by the Markac Defence. We received a submission, defendant Mladen Markac motion to have one of Witness 81's statement deemed inadmissible; but it deals, as a matter of fact, with the expansion of the scope of testimony for Witness 116. These are two different witnesses. On the first page, we find defendant Mladen Markac to have, one, Witness 81's statement deemed inadmissible, but then it continues about Witness 116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand that although the date is 20th of June, that it was filed this morning. Mr. Kuzmanovic, any reason on why there was a reason to mix up two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What ended up happening was when it got sent, somehow it got -- the face page got mistranscribed, and we'll correct it; however, this morning, Mr. Misetic will address the other portion of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, it is not just the cover page. It is also the first page where we have two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that the submission is about Witness 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Their submission is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, our submission is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record, we, the Gotovina Defence, will be filing a motion to strike the second 92 ter statement that is referenced in the caption, which will hopefully filed in the next day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second 92 ter statement of Witness 116?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 81, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, today, we are dealing with Witness 116, so 81 will --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Will wait, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- will wait until we've done with this one. Then I also do understand that the there were no objections against the admission of statements and exhibits, apart from the last two ones, two maps to be exhibited, where I think it was the Gotovina Defence who said it is irrelevant; and if it would be admitted, we'd need one more day for cross-examination. Mr. Tieger, is there anything you'd like to -- you have already responded to that, saying that it is relevant. The main issue seems to be that you say that whatever policy was there in view of Bosnia is irrelevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That also includes not just the maps but the transcript of the 29 October 1993 matter. If I may, Judge, on various different levels, obviously it -- 1993 has got very little to do with this case. It certainly has nothing that connects it to our client General Gotovina. And, probably, the most significant issue here with regard to this is it is actually a matter which will impeach the Prosecution's witness, Ambassador Galbraith. If the theory on bring this matter in, especially the whole discussion in 1993, that President Tudjman had some idea to cleanse the area of Serbs and he engaged in a methodology on that score, which is, I assume, what the Prosecution is attempt to go bring this in, that is undercut, not only undercut, but eliminated by this witness in paragraph 81, where he notes in the first line: "I don't think it was Tudjman's plan to expel all Serbs from Croatia." That's the second-to-last paragraph in his statement. That being said, Your Honours, number 1, it certainly well outside the time-frame of this indictment; number 2, there is nothing whatsoever linking any comments by President Tudjman at any time-frame to General Gotovina; and, number 3, the admission of this evidence is impeaching their own witness, which, Your Honour, quite frankly, under Rule 90 is improper. I mean, the Prosecution is allowed to put their case on and their cases comes from this particular witness, but impeaching their own witness is yet a different matter. So, suffice it to say, just based on the first line in paragraph 91 alone, there's really no relevance to this particular line of inquiry on Bosnia and what President Tudjman's comments were on Bosnia. I note, Your Honour, that the entire matter of President Tudjman and Bosnia has been the subject of the Prlic case, which I believe started sometime 2007, and it looks destined to end sometime in the latter part of 2009. So we're talking about an extremely complex issue which has been highly debated in another forum within the ICTY. I don't think we need get that fair, Judge. The fact of the matter is that it has absolutely no relevance to this case, and this particular witness is going to say that in his -- in paragraph 91 [sic], exactly what he outlined before, that it wasn't Tudjman's plan to expel all Serbs from Croatia. Now, the other aspect to this, Judge, and a matter which we also take in on Rule 90(H) is the matter of probative value verse prejudice. I mean, what is the probative value of this particular line of inquiry vis-a-vis the prejudice that will emanate to our client, especially when the Prosecution has got absolutely nothing to tie General Gotovina to this item. Given those circumstances, Judge, what I have just outlined, the time-frame, the lack the relevance, the lack of connection, and the fact that this particular witness undercuts this is entire theory, especially vis-a-vis Operation Storm, there's simply no reason to allow this item into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, before we continue, I see "paragraph 91." On the transcript, I think I heard you say "81," and that seems to be more in line with your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it was. Tudjman's plan appears in 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 81. If I said "91," I meat "81." I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know where the mistake was, but let's proceed. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I spoke too quickly as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just correct one other item. What I was talking about on the prejudicial -- the probative value being outweighed by the prejudicial effect is Rule 89(D). I misspoke and talked about Rule 90; it's Rule 89(D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence argument concerning these issues appears to conflate several matters. I don't know if I can you think tangle them, but let me try quickly. First of all, the allegation that, for example, the 1993 transcript is untimely because it is early, or because it demonstrates no explicit link to the accused, does not go to the issue for which that document was produced and the witness's comments about them. The witness offers extensive testimony about the position and attitudes of the Croatian leadership toward the continued presence of Serbs in the Krajina. He explains and will explain to the Court the basis for his understanding of those views. That includes his deals with the Croatia leadership from the commencement of his term as ambassador. That document points to an expression of views that is consistent with and that form part of the basis for his assessment of President Tudjman's views about multi-national states, about the need for ethnic homogeneity in a state and its resultant implications for actions that were taken in connection with this case. This is not an attempt to criminal responsibility for actions in Central Bosnia. The fact that there may be some overlap with another case currently ongoing in this institution does not mean that the Court should be precluded from hearing evidence that is relevant to this case. And, clearly, evidence of President Tudjman's views and the views of other Croatian leaders about such issues as ethnic homogeneity, population transfers, and the like, is relevant to this Court, and should be heard. In so far as impeaching one's witness is concerned, I think the Court is entitled. First of, all this is not an impeachment. Defence quotes one passage of the witness's statement. It is clear that that statement continues: He didn't start out in 1991 to do this. It also goes on: That had the Serb population remained, policies would have been such to make them leave. There are other portions of his statement and of his anticipated evidence that will make clear the policies that were implemented in the Krajina to ensure that Serbs did not return and to ensure a largely homogeneous state. All of this evidence is of clear relevance to this case, and should be heard by the Court. In so far as the balance of the evidence to the potential prejudice, there's no attempt here to, as I say, litigate the issue of criminal responsibility for a Central Bosnia. The Court is clearly capable of segregating these issues to the extent that witness received information and that is relevant to this case. And, certainly, as I have mentioned, the positions and attitudes of the Croatian leadership, and particularly President Tudjman, concerning Serbs and ethnic homogeneity is relevant and, indeed, should be heard. And the Court can easily separate those issues, particularly in light of the fact that the emphasis will be on the issues I have mentioned and not -- not criminal responsibility for actions in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respectfully. First of all, as Your Honour was pointing out the obvious, I mean, President Tudjman is not on trial hear. Of course, the reason that the Prosecution wants to put this is in is to somehow link this up to General Gotovina and somehow have this item out is there that is some kind of overflow on to General Gotovina with absolutely no evidence whatsoever. And if that is clearly what is envisaged in 89(D), when we talk about prejudice outweighed by the probative value, what other reason could there be for the Prosecution to put this in, if it wasn't to somehow bring General Gotovina in to this when there is no evidence whatsoever? Now I will tell you, Judge, that the time involved in answering President Tudjman's views in Bosnia and all the matters that are coming in is just an enormous undertaking. I mean, logistically here - I know time is a concern to Your Honours - logistically here, it is physically impossible a this juncture to meet that. I mean, if this goes forward in this fashion, in the way that the Prosecution wants to propose it, then it is going to significantly lengthen this matter and possibly call this witness back at some other juncture, but certainly lengthen any case as we develop this matter with witnesses to come. I don't know how far that's going to go time-wise. But, suffice it to say, the simply matter here, as a result of paragraph 81 - and this case involves Operation Storm. It doesn't involve Bosnia, it doesn't involve all these other matters, it involves Operation Storm - is that Tudjman didn't have any intent to cleanse the Croats -- excuse me, the Serbs from Croatia. Now, if that's the case, as we move into Operation Storm, that there was no intent to exclude the Serbs from Croatia, and this is a matter with which General Gotovina is called do answer these charges, how is this other matter relevant to a case against General Gotovina? Not President Tudjman, or not some other leader that has not been charged; General Gotovina. How is that relevant? Nothing the Prosecution has just said, in the speech they just gave, answers that very crucial question: The link to this man and his right to answer that particular evidence. This is going way far afield to try to bring in evidence that simply doesn't exist linking General Gotovina to any idea of expelling Serbs from Croatia. It simply doesn't. And if the Prosecution has that evidence, let's deal with that evidence. Let put that on the table right now, so General Gotovina through his counsel can answer it; not through these innuendos and allegations and 1993 conversations, especially in light of this comment by Ambassador Galbraith who was here at the time who said that Tudjman had no such intent certainly as it pertained to Operation Storm. It is just an enormous undertaking that they have thrown before this Chamber that if allowed to pursue, it is going to take an enormous effort to answer. I don't want to engage in hyperbolic arguments, Judge, but I raised the Prlic matter simply because that is what they have been doing for the past two years. But it all comes down to relevance, some connection to General Gotovina; and in light of what Ambassador Galbraith said that there was no intent by Tudjman to exclude the Serbs from Croatia, this is a non-issue in this particular Chamber and this particular case with regard to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'd like to add something to this discussion, and that is this: I'd like to know when the decision was made to enter into this discussion by the Prosecution of using ethnic maps through Ambassador Galbraith, because the first notice we got of this was on June 20 when this exhibit showed up on our e-mails, and an e-mail exchange occurred between counsel for General Gotovina and Mr. Tieger about this subject. It's not as if this was something that we were received notice of and had plenty of time to prepare for and knew something about in advance. This was something that was thrust upon us at the last minute, an entirely huge issue, involving, as Mr. Kehoe said - I'm not going to repeat what he said - but, obviously, a number of complicated facts and opinions and about a person who is not on trial. So, you know, this case is about Operation Storm and the relevant responsibilities, if any, of these defendants for the acts alleged in the indictment; not something that happened in Bosnia occurring around discussion in 1993 through a witness who really has, in my view, nothing to do with my particular client in terms of what he says in his statement, or it is just general background information which really isn't necessary. And as far as I'm concerned, it runs far afield from the issues of the indictment in this case relevant to these clients in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we hear from the Cermak Defence whether they --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It seems that the scope that the Prosecution are using in relation to this matter falls outside the ambit of the case that is on trial here concerning Operation Storm. And it is quite clear from what they are doing, they are seeking to provide foundation from elsewhere in support of their argument in relation to Operation Storm but not directly related to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a while to consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't have a chance to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree, but I also had in mind to ask the other Defence counsel to give their views. They've done so, meanwhile. But if an objection is made, if it is in response to Mr. Kehoe, usually you ask -- you just do not respond yet, but you ask whether there is a second round of argument. That is not a drama here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, then, I think it is also fair to give Mr. Tieger a brief opportunity; although, I did not hear much new argument, Mr, Tieger, so if you could keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very short, Your Honour. First of all, three matters, I guess, quickly: Number one, the attempt to disentangle President Tudjman from this case is clearly in opposite, and would be, in any event; but clearly so by virtue of the fact that there is a JCE allegation. Number 2, Mr. Kehoe said part of the argument is based on the fact that the witness's testimony is that there was no intent to exclude Serbs from Croatia. I think his evidence is quite to the contrary, and the Courts needs to here that. Number 3, as far as the maps are concerned, they are practically matters that could be judicially noticed. There were only put on the exhibit list to provide clarification to the Court in so far as was necessary based on witness evidence. It doesn't involve new matters, and it arises directly from information that is part of the witness's proposed 92 ter statement and supplemental information. It is nothing new and was only an attempt to provide, if necessary, any visual assistance to the Court about the matters raised in the statement itself in so far as boundaries were discussed, and in so far as particular locations, and some particular locations are, indeed, mentioned where the witness travelled, are raised. So nothing new was raised by those maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, because, of, course the Chamber has not seen the maps, are these the kind of maps that were produced on the basis of the 1991 census which we have seen in other cases and just gives percentages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the matter. --- Break taken at 9.28 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objections based on lack of relevance and impeachment of the own witness. Mr. Tieger, at the same time, the mindset of those who participated in the joint criminal enterprise in earlier stages is not of vital importance. I mean, we should focus not on the background, so we should avoid that what is naturally as a background should not become the foreground. So, therefore, the Chamber is not interested to hear evidence on everything that happened in Bosnia. As far as impeachment is concerned, especially if you look at paragraph 91, Mr. Kehoe very much stressed the first sentence of that paragraph; and, of course, that paragraph says more than just what are not the plans of Mr. Tudjman, who is in the indictment one of the participants in the joint criminal enterprise. Of course, he is not an accused in this case, but he is in the indictment part of the joint criminal enterprise. So his development of thoughts and what he later may have done, whether or not together with the accused is still to be established, is not lacking all evidence. Then, finally, the maps. The maps, the Chamber grants your request to add them to the 65 ter list. At the same time, the Chamber will consider what the relevance of those maps is when it comes to the testimony and when these maps will be introduced through this witness. As I said before, the Chamber had not seen the maps. Meanwhile, we have looked at a copy, and it seems it is the ethnic composition of Bosnia; and, therefore, we would have to establish a clear link with this case, this case which is I wouldn't say an entirely out of Bosnia. I mean, they are close to the border. Things happened over there which also have some or may have some bearing on this case, but the whole ethnic map of Bosnia seems not to be foreground information. So, the Chamber reserves its position in this respect until these maps are tendered into evidence through this witness. Any other matters at this moment? If not, then, first of all, I see, Ms. Schildge, you're present in the courtroom. That is on the basis of the decision and the request made. Ms. Schildge, perhaps, one question. The Chamber decided last week on the basis of a letter presented by the Gotovina Defence that the scope of the cross-examination would a bit expanded if we compare it with the earlier decision. I see you're nodding yes. We have not considered one moment that this letter was not a true letter from the US government; so, therefore, we grant it on the basis of this confidence. We granted the decision. And if that would be otherwise, then, of course, we would like to hear from you. But from your body language at this moment, it appears there is no problem in this respect. Then, Mr. Tieger, are you ready to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The Prosecution calls Ambassador Peter Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I see that a corrigendum was filed on the 23rd of June in relation to the issue I raised earlier; that is, about the issue of the submission dated 20th of June, and I might have been mistaken when I said it was filed the 23rd of June. I haven't seen the original registration page. I see now that at least the corrigendum was filed on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you to put on your headphones, not because you wouldn't understand the English language, but sometimes we get messages from the interpreter's booth. Mr. Galbraith, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The usher now hands out the text of this solemn declaration, and I ask to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Galbraith. Mr. Galbraith, if I address you as "Mr. Galbraith," and not as "Ambassador Galbraith," that is because I have developed a habit that everyone who appears in this courtroom, irrespective of rank, position, et cetera, is here just as a person. It has got nothing to do with disrespect. Everyone does it the way he wants to do it. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be examined by Mr. Tieger who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will break that egalitarian tradition, as is common with lawyers, and say good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Good morning. You know how it is with titles. The title plus two euros, I can ride the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me begin by, first of all, ask you to state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Peter Woodward Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to provide the Court with some quick snapshot of your background. If I may, I will just recite some of the highlights and ask you to affirm those if I have stated them correctly. You were educated at Harvard, Oxford, and Georgetown universities, receiving a bachelor's degree from Harvard, a masters from Oxford, and a law degree from Georgetown university. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Following that, you had a career as the senior advisor to the United States Senate, foreign relations committee from 1979 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the latter period of your work as senior advisor, you had a mandate to deal with the difficult locations in the world; and in the course of that effort, paid four visits to the region of the former Yugoslavia in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as a result of that, you reported to the committee regarding ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were appointed as the United States ambassador to Croatia, indeed, the first United States ambassador to the independent Republic of Croatia, in June of 1992 and served until January 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just catching up very quickly, since that time, you have taught for some years at the United States -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you say June of 1992? It would be June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I may have misspoken. Thanks for that correction. You taught at the United States National War College from 1988 to 2003?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, although with a period in East Timor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that work in East Timor was as the director for political, constitutional, and electoral affairs for the United Nations in East Timor, where you became the cabinet member for political affairs when the interim government was formed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could presented to the witness 65 ter 5206. Perhaps, I could ask -- well, I see the usher is well ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it there is no problem that the witness has his statements in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, although the problem with the pace of speech has been exclusively mine, I do want to remind you to pause between question and answer to allow the interpreters to catch up, and I will also try to deliberately speak closer to ease their task as well. Ambassador, looking at this exhibit before you now, is this a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you review this document before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect the information that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is the information contained in that statement true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is, subject to the supplemental -- some corrections made in the supplemental statement that I prepared in interviews with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you were asked about the same matters here in Court today, subject to the caveat you have just mentioned, would the information you provided be the same?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also like to present the supplemental information sheet to the witness, and that is 65 ter 5235.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ambassador, does this document contain the corrections to your earlier statement that you mentioned, as well as supplemental information concerning that statement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review this document before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect the information that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is the information contained in that document true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you were asked about the same matters here in Court today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My inquiry on the main statement of the witness is when it was actually finalised. Obviously, this is not signed. I don't have a signed copy. I don't think one was ever produced. It notes date of interviews, but doesn't note any date of finalisation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cover page, Mr. Tieger, says the 5th of February. I think it was 22nd of February -- no. It say the 5th of February, 2008. It gives dates of interview is 22 February and 13 April 2007. I don't know what explains the 5th of February, 2008 date, which I find on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The finalisation, as it were, occurred at or about the time of the date shown on the document itself. The ambassador reviewed and approved the contents of the document sometime relatively shortly before that. There was, indeed, a period of time between - a significant period of time, indeed - between the date of the last interview and the finalisation of the document; not through any fault of the witness, simply because of the hope there would be an additional opportunities to address issues. Then the imminence and the trial date meant the document had to be finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My questioned was when it was formalised, Judge. Normally - and I am not a stickler for procedure - but, normally, we have a signature page to say that the witness signed off at a particular time. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I think the witness just testified that this is the statement he gave. This replaces his signature, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Peter Galbraith was the United States ambassador to Croatia from 24 June 1993 to 3 January 1998. In that capacity, he had extensive contacts with members of the Croatian leadership, Krajina Serb leadership, international representatives, and others dealing with the region. Ambassador Galbraith was active in attempting to broker a peaceful settlement between Croatia and the Krajina Serbs, including the Z-4 plan. As Operation Storm became imminent, he met with President Tudjman on 1 August 1995, and advised President Tudjman to take care in protecting Serb civilians and UN personnel if an attack was launched. On the 2nd of August, Ambassador Galbraith met with Milan Babic to convince him to accept terms for peace. Babic agreed to conditions. And on the 3rd of August, as negotiations in Geneva were taking place, Ambassador Galbraith met with President Tudjman to explain his meeting with Babic and the opportunity for a peaceful solution. President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Tieger. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: President Tudjman expressed skepticism that Babic could deliver, and it was clear to Ambassador Galbraith that the attack would go forward. During the course of his work, Ambassador Galbraith had regular and extensive contact with President Tudjman and other Croatian leaders, and learned of their attitudes and positions regarding the presence of Serbs in Croatia. President Tudjman believed that states should be ethnically homogeneous or close to it. He believed and stated that the Serbs in Croatia, and particularly the Krajina, were too numerous and constituted a strategic threat to Croatia. He approved of population transfers to create largely homogeneous states or areas. President Tudjman also had racist views towards Muslims. President Tudjman considered that his arguments about Serbs and Muslims were irresistible, and he, therefore, did not need to mask these views. After Operation Storm, President Tudjman explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: President Tudjman explained clearly to Ambassador Galbraith that the Serbs that had left should not come back. Measures were imposed to ensure that the Serbs would not, in fact, return, including laws confiscating property and preventing people from returning after giving them only 30 days to do so. Although that deadline was extended under pressure, means were imposed to prevent Serbs from meeting those deadlines and making it impossible to reclaim property. Meanwhile, a large part of Serb property was being systematically destroyed by Croatian armed forces and others. Ambassador Galbraith received information from many sources about the crimes and about the extensive and systematic destruction of Serb property and about widespread killings. His own observations were consistent with those reports. Ambassador Galbraith assessed that such destruction could not have taken place without the orders, approval, or acquiescence of Croatian leadership. He constantly raised with Croatian leaders the issue of crimes against Serbs and Serb property, and the obstacles imposed against Serb return. In response, there was first stonewalling and denial, and then grudging acknowledgment or deflections, such as asserting that Croat civilians returning to the area were doing it and that it was outside the control of the officials. Although pressure by the international community over time had some positive effect over the time, particularly on the right of return and the destruction diminished, by the end almost all had listen looted and/or destroyed. That concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, welcome back. We've indicated already that you began your term as ambassador in June of 1993. Can I ask you, then, to describe to the Court the prevailing conditions at that time and their impact on your focus of activities and your priorities?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The war in the former Yugoslavia had been going on for two years. 29 per cent of the territory of the Republic of Croatia was occupied by rebel Serbs who were backed by Serbia. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a three-way war between the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian government, and the HVO. There were hundreds of thousands of refugees in Croatia, perhaps six or 700.000, who had passed through Croatia; and the international community, including my own government, were frankly despairing as to what might be done about this situation. I arrived as the first ambassador actually in circumstances where the United States was on the verge of not sending an ambassador to protest what Croatia was doing in Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, it's support for the HVO which was fighting and committing atrocities against the troops -- against the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian government. And so my initial focus -- well, the first point I would say is that I realised that there was going to be no solution to this conflict, unless we could end the fighting between the Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia. So that was the first focus of my activities. And in order -- before we could end the fighting, we had to end the atrocities. And, so, in the summer of 1993, I worked with Croatian officials to get Bosnian prisoners released from camps where they were being held in inhumane conditions, to try and stop the shelling of Mostar, and to reduce the level of atrocities. In 1994, the focus -- or in late 1993/1994, the focus shifted to try and arrange a peace agreement between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Croats; and we succeeded at the end of February, beginning of March of 1994, when we concluded the Washington agreement that created the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and which immediately and successfully ended the Muslim-Croat war. At that point, at the request of President Tudjman, I turned my attention to negotiations with -- between Zagreb and rebel Serbs in Knin, to try and find a political settlement in Croatia. Those negotiations had been ongoing under the auspices of the United Nations. The Russians got involved, and Tudjman wanted the Americans to be involved. I eventually formed a group with the United Nations, the Russians, and the European Union. It became known as Zagreb 4, or Z-4, and we sponsored a three part process to try to find a peaceful settlement in Croatia. First was a cease-fire which was successfully negotiated in March of 1994. That was followed by agreement on economic and confidence building measures in December of 1994. And parallel to the economic and confidence building measures, we worked up a political plan, which became known as the Z-4 plan, that would have provided for very substantial autonomy for the Krajina Serbs within the internationally recognised borders of Croatia. That plan was presented to the parties, not only as a document to be negotiated about, not on a take it or leave it basis, that was presented in January of 1995. President Tudjman very reluctantly accepted it and agreed to negotiate on it, but the leader of the Krajina Serbs, Milan Martic, refused to touch the document. He refused to receive it. And at that point, the negotiations between the two sides broke down, as it turned out, irretrievably; although, I made efforts to try and get them started again. In the summer, or in May to July of 1995, things began really to fall apart. UN peacekeepers were taken in hostage; then and in July came the attacks on the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, which fell; and then an attack on Bihac, which was carried out both by the Bosnian Serb army and by the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, that is, the rebel Croats. And at that point, the Croatian government took the decision that -- that this was the opportune time to move militarily to recover Croatian territory, and a series of events - I could describe in more detail - but a series of events set in motion which led to Operation Storm.

I think the date the day I became -- well, I was first told that there was going to be an operation was the day that I took the defence attache, Colonel Rick Herrick, over for his farewell call with Defence Minister Gojko Susak and his replacement, Colonel John Sadler. And at that time, either at that meeting or at a lunch at the Intercon in Zagreb, Susak told me of the plans for a military attack on the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can just sharpen this date, I think the diary reflects June 10th on page 12, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me clarify. I knew substantially before June 10th, and this is reflected in lots of documents, that it was Tudjman's plan in 1994 to take the Krajina militarily. As is true for the entry on this date, we believed that he would do this when the United Nations mandate ran out November 30th. The reason being that that would be a time of the year when it would be very difficult for weather reasons for Serbia to resupply the Krajina, but where it would be still relatively easy for Croatian forces to attack up from the coast and where it wouldn't do any damage to the Croatian tourist season. It was later in July, because of what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa and because of the Bihac crisis, that these plans were advanced to take advantage of the -- well, for two reasons: First, to save Bihac. The last things that the Croatians wanted was for Bihac to fall, and then you would have a single western Serb entity, Krajina and Bosnia. You would also have 160.000 people who would be going to Croatia as refugees. And I have to tell, although I am sure this will come up in the further testimony, it was the last thing that the United States wanted to see either. But the decision to do it in July was not -- Croatia did not advance the date of this operation until after Srebrenica and until the Bihac crisis. And, so, I believe that I was told a very short period of time after Croatia had made the tentative decision. I don't think it made the final decision, well, if you look at the transcript, even up until the day before; but it was around the 20th of July that they made the initial decision that this was the time to do it.
