utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin, I'd like to indicate to the Court that it appears that one of the pages of the diplomatic diary was not copied in e-court, and that's the page that is marked on the diary, 29, which appeared -- which would have appeared between page 22 and page 23 of the e-court version. The pages marked in the diary don't correspond precisely to e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, apparently, the hard copy that was sent has the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I have copies here. Fortunately, I know that I checked with Mr. Kehoe, he does have that page in the copy of the diary he has. But if other counsel need a copy or for the benefit of the Court, I have copies of that particular missing page now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have it, that saves us from printing it. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do have that. My issue is on a different subject that I did address with Mr. Tieger concerning the transcript, and just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This seems not to deal with authenticity, but rather by error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. The authenticity issue we will address yet further after I get some additional information. But by way of clarity, Your Honour, on page 34, line 19, I believe there is some concern about the date on that line, and the year. I may have misheard the witness, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not at all sure that that is an error, but I would be happy to clarify it with the witness. I think that is the best way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the best way to do it; otherwise, Mr. Kehoe still has an opportunity in cross-examination to deal with the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As long as it was raised, Mr. Ambassador, let me take to you the portion of the transcript. As indicated, that was page 34. The question was -- you are attempting to sharpen the date. When you first learn that there would be a military operation to retake the Krajina, you said beginning at line 17: "Let me clarify. I knew substantially before June 10, and this is reflected in lots of documents, that it was Tudjman's plan in 1994 to take the Krajina militarily." And you went on: "As is true for the entry on this date, we believe that they would do so -- do this when the United Nations mandate ran out November 30th," and then it goes on. So the question is, Ambassador: Did you mean 1994 or some other date?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I meant 1995; that is, that the UN mandate ran from March - it was eight months - I think from March until the end of November. It was at that point, in 1995, that Tudjman's plan was to take the Krajina. As long as we're on this subject, I realise I made another point that merits clarification on exactly this issue. It was on the 21st of July that I went down to Brioni - this is 1995 - for a dinner with President Demirel. And at that dinner, Susak, the defence minister, told me that they would have a military operation. It was later, I think July 22nd, looking at the diary, that I had the lunch that I referred to with Colonel Herrick and Colonel Sadler. And on that occasion, Susak gave us the date. But it would have been on the 21st that he had first indicated to me, and it was also clear from what Tudjman was saying that Tudjman had made a decision that they were going to go ahead with a military operation -- or very likely to go ahead with a military operation in connection with the Bihac crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Now, in connection with the Bihac crisis, that's also mentioned in your statement, I think at paragraphs 19 -- that's 92 ter statement, P444, at paragraphs 19 and 20, in which you indicate that: "During the same period, the threat to Bihac lessened in the face of Serb withdrawal," at paragraph 19. And then in paragraph 20: "Now we move again to start again the peace progress. There was a hierarchy of evil." Can you describe to the Court, quickly, the reduction of the threat to Bihac and the efforts in connection with the peace process that resulted?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, what happened was you had on the 13th of July, the fall of Srebrenica; then the disappearance and massacre of 20 per cent of the population, the men and boys; then you had the fall of Zepa around the 26th of July, but the attack on it had been going on for some time; and in around the 20th or 17th, or something, of July, the attack on Bihac. So, as we saw it, there was a concerted effort on the part of the Bosnian Serbs, and in the case of the Bihac joined by the Croatian Serbs, to wipe these enclaves off the map. And we believe, given what they had done in Srebrenica, that there was a very good chance that they would do the same thing in Zepa and in Bihac. That is why we were very sympathetic to the Croatian military offensive that went up the Livno valley that put pressure on the Serbs, and, indeed, why we did not object to military action that would have come through the Krajina to relieve the siege of Bihac. But precisely because the Croatian military actions were having a significant impact on the Serbs, the prospect of Bihac falling had, by the very end of July, began to recede. And at that point, I believed that there was an opportunity to -- for a negotiated settlement. I wasn't at all sure that there would be a negotiated settlement that would actually work, but that there was an opportunity and that we should take advantage of this opportunity. That then explains why, at the very final hours, I went to Belgrade and tried to produce a deal that might have headed off Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your statement -- your statement indicates , at paragraph 22, and again that's P444, at paragraph 22, that you met with President Tudjman on the 1st of August; and, I believe, in addition your diplomatic diary, at the page marked 28, which I think is page 22 in e-court, also addresses that meeting. During the course of that meeting with President Tudjman, Ambassador, did you outline the proposal to move the peace process forward, and did you also address US concerns about a military operation and the US position in connection with that possibility?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does your -- does your diary and your statement indicate the position outlined by you, on behalf of the US, in connection with the possibility of a military operation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those were?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, first, that the United States was committed to a peaceful solution to the Krajina problem, and that nothing that we said should be construed as a green light to military operation. Second, and we put great emphasis on this, that if there is a military operation, that Serb civilians will have to be protected; that POWs will have to be well treated; and that any repeat of the atrocities that had occurred in the Medak Pocket in 1993 would have very series consequences for US/Croatian relations. If there were atrocities, that would very much affect our relationship in a negative, do great damage to our relationship with Croatia. Third, if Croatia undertook a military operation, that it would do so alone. It could not expect any help from the United States if things did not go as expected. And, fourth, that the safety of UN peacekeepers was paramount, and that Croatia would have to avoid doing anything that put UN peacekeepers and other personnel at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 23 of P444, you explained the reasons why warnings were issued about the need to protect Serb civilians. You say: "I issued the warnings about the need to protect Serbian civilians because there were a number of reasons to be worried that persecutions of civilians were likely. I knew that President Tudjman saw Serbs as a threat and wanted an ethnically homogeneous Croatia. I also knew that Serbia civilians had been attacked in previous Croatian military operations such as Medak Pocket and Flash." Then you go on to indicate that your concern was reflected in a statement later. Does that paragraph accurately state the reasons why the warnings about the need or US concern about what might happen to civilians were issued?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in the meeting on August 1st, did President Tudjman outline for you the conditions, Croatia's conditions, for a peaceful resolution in anticipation of your meeting with Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He outlined the conditions for a peaceful resolution, which are contained in the diplomatic diary; that is, the immediate withdrawal from Bihac, the opening of the oil pipeline through Sector North, immediate negotiations to reopen the Zagreb-Split railroad, and immediate negotiations for the political reintegration of the Krajina into Croatia. At that time, these were his conditions and these were being presented as an ultimatum at a meeting to be held August 3rd in Geneva under the sponsorship the ICVY, the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, and under the chairmanship of Thorvald Stoltenberg. At that time, then I told him that Babic was interested in seeing me, and he said, "Well, that would be interesting." I think Babic had proposed a date of Thursday or Friday, and he said, "Don't wait until then; do it sooner." But these points were not in connection with my meeting with Babic, these were simply the Croatian ultimatum, and the focus really was on that August 3rd meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you meet with Milan Babic thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I met with him on the 2nd of August in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. With what result? Did you outline the conditions that had presented to you, and what was the response?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I painted -- I began the meeting by painting the starkest picture of what was likely to happen, and I put the blame very squarely on the Krajina Serbs who had done two things: First, they had crossed the international border into Bihac; and, second, they had refused to negotiate on the basis of a proposal that was with put forward by the United States, Russia, the United Nations, and the European Union. That is, basically, the most powerful institutions in the world, at least with regard to that part of the world. Then I outlined to him the Croatian conditions, and his response was very interesting. I expected him to argue, but he didn't. He said: "I understand completely why the Croatians are about to attack us. I cannot understand why our leaders have behaved as they -- they do." He said that he accepted Tudjman's ultimatum, all the points. He said, "Except, I have difficulty in publically saying that I will accept negotiations for the reintegration of the Krajina into Croatia." And, so, I said to him, "Well, I thought about that, and what I think you can do is publicly announce that you will accept negotiations on the basis of the Z-4 plan, because the Z-4 plan is a plan for the reintegration of Krajina into Croatia. But I need to tell Tudjman privately that you understand you will never get the level of autonomy that was discussed in the Z-4 plan. What might have been possible in January of 1995 is not possible in August of 1995." He said he understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I may have been remiss in not asking you earlier to indicate to the Court who Milan Babic was, why you were dealing with him, and -- well, I think it is clear.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Milan Babic was the prime minister of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina; that is, the rebel Serb entity. He also headed the political party that had the most popular support in the Krajina. That was a majority in the parliament. He was, however, a political opponent Milan Martic, the president, who controlled the military and, therefore, exercised substantially more power than Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your supplemental statement, I believe -- supplemental information sheet, excuse me. That is P445, and I believe it indicates, at paragraph 18, your review of the transcript of August 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I should indicate that the ambassador in an opportunity to see a revised transcript that conforms to an issue raised during the opening statement, and contains the translation, a revised translation, of the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, as indicated in P445, Ambassador, that indicates that as you were relating to -- and I should indicate for your benefit and the Court, this is a transcript of a meeting with President Tudjman, in which you related your discussion with Milan Babic. You. Are quoted there as saying: "As we know very well, that many Serbs living there would leave, probably the majority of them. Do you recall indicating that to President Tudjman and to Milan Babic earlier; and if so, can you explain why you said to Babic that many Serbs, probably the majority of them would leave? And as I indicated, that is addressed at page 18 of P445, the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. The point I was trying to make to Babic is that if the Krajina Serb population was gone, there would never be a political settlement for them, and so they were much better off to accept a deal with Croatia now, even if it was far from ideal from their specific, than to have the marry solved militarily and then to have the entire population leave. Now, why did I say to him, to Babic, that I thought the entire population would leave? Well, because through the entire conflict in the former Yugoslavia when territory changed hands, populations left or were expelled; because when Croatia took over Western Slavonia in May 1 and 2, of 1995, just a few months before, 10.000 of the 13.000 Serbs left there; because of Croatia's conduct in previous operations had, in particular, Medak Pocket, had involved atrocities. So I knew the population would have a well-founded fear of what might happen. I knew Tudjman's own statements and view that the Krajina Serbs were a strategic threat to Croatia, and I also knew the relentless Serb propaganda about how the Croatians were basically born-again Ustashi, World War II fascist, who repeat all atrocities of the Ustashi. So it was the combination of all those things that led me to say to Babic that the Serb would say leave. But Babic was -- I didn't have to persuade him of this. He understood completely that this was going to happen. Then with Tudjman, on the 3rd of August, I was simply recounting to him the -- the entirety of my conversation with Babic, so he would understand how we had gotten this deal in which Babic had, in my view, accepted Tudjman's ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned your meeting with President Tudjman following your discussion with Milan Babic. How did you present the situation as it existed at that time to President Tudjman, and what was his reaction? I believe that is found in or you address those issues to some extent at paragraph 26 of your statement, and pages 31 through 32 of your diary as marked on the diary page, which I believe would be page 24 of the e-court version, the August 3rd meeting.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: My basic -- I mean, of course, the words are reflected in the diary and, as you know, in the transcript. But my basic message was that Babic had accepted Tudjman's ultimatum, that we could not know whether Babic was going to be able to deliver the Krajina Serb leadership, but that it was worth taking a little bit of time to find out if he would. That was -- that basically is what I was trying to persuade Tudjman of. I just described my own negotiations, and I also delivered a demarche on behalf of the United States. It was clear to me -- I think I saw Tudjman at 5.45. It was clear to me that what I was saying was falling on deaf ears. He was -- I believed he had already made the decision to go to war. It was interesting for me, then, to read the transcript of the subsequent national security meeting that began at 6.00, where the issue was actually debated and they did give considerable -- they did give consideration to the American demarche and what I had to say. But, certainly, the impression I had at that meeting was that the issue was settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you -- subsequently, did you in connection with that issue hold a press conference - I believe that is addressed at pages 208 through 210 of the book, "The United States and Croatia: A Documentary History" - about the opportunity presented as a result of your discussions with Babic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I felt we should do everything possible for peace. So, typically, when I would go see, Tudjman - or frequently anyhow - the press would be gathered out the presidential office. I actually had our public affairs officer make sure that they were there. So I then issued a statement, saying that Babic had meet Tudjman's -- it was wasn't a statement. I gave remarks that Babic had met the terms of Croatia's ultimatum; and that, in my view, there was no reason for a war. I didn't say there wouldn't be a war, although that was a bit misinterpreted. I simply said that there was no reason for way. I also felt, as a moral matter, that I owed it to Babic who had made this commitments to state publicly that the United States stood behind them, and that we hoped there would be an opportunity for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you referred, both in connection with the reasons why you issued the warnings to President Tudjman about Serb civilians and I believe earlier in your testimony, to President Tudjman's views of the presence of Serbs in Croatia. Let me ask you, as a preliminary matter, how frequently and regularly you met with President Tudjman during the -- your term as ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In the first two and a half years, I met with him very frequently; I would say several times a week, on some occasions several times a day. Not all these would have been meetings at his office. We would have met in other places. I went down; and when he vacationed in Brioni, I went down from time to time to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you also describe the frequency of your meetings with other leading Croatian officials and who some of those leading people were?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: My closest contacts were with Defence Minister Gojko Susak, who I simply saw all the time, and this was a fast-moving situation. I suppose I saw him four or five times a week, sometimes more. We often spoke; and Foreign Minister Mate Granic, whose ministry was just across the park, maybe a one-minute walk from the American embassy. Again, I would see him four or five times a week. We would speak on the phone all the time. The other official that I dealt with -- among the other officials I dealt with a lot were Hrvoje Sarinic who, was Tudjman's Chief of Staff and who was became the lead Croatian negotiator on the Eastern Slavonia peace agreement, which is a set of negotiations that followed Operation Storm that I was the mediator of; Miro Tudjman, Tudjman's son, who was head of the Croatian intelligence service. I saw him somewhat less frequently; Djurdja Susak, who was Miro's deputy and the wife of the Defence minister. And, of course, there were many others, but the big three would have been Granic, Susak, and Sarinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In P444, your 92 ter statement, in paragraphs 31 through 31, you address President Tudjman's views on a number of related subjects, including his belief that states ought to be ethnically homogeneous or close to it, his belief and statements that Serbs in Croatia were to numerous and constituted a strategic threat to Croatia, his views about population transfers, his views that the Krajina Serbs represented, as I think I mentioned, a strategic threat. Can you describe for the Court, in as much -- in any more detail than is necessary, those views on both the continued presence of Serbs in Croatia and population transfers and ethnic division.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: First, I think a word about Tudjman. He was an extremely confident leader, very confident in his own abilities. He was a historian by academic training. He was a strategist, but he thought of himself as a strategist on a grand scale. He had strongly-held beliefs which he felt would be self-evident to a rational Westerner, like the American ambassador. So he never hid his views. And he believed that states were -- European states were much better off if they were ethnically homogeneous. Kind of an odd argument for him to think that an American, given the nature of our country, would believe that, but he just assumed that I would accept that. He saw because of their geography that the Krajina Serbs were a particular threat. They were located, after all, in such a way that they almost divided the northern part of Croatia from the coast. He, as a historian, he spoke about approvingly of population transfers, particularly the population transfer that took place in 1923 after the Greek-Turkish War, in which the Greek population of Anatolia was sent to and Greece, and the Turkish population in Greece was sent to Turkey. Although I would argue with him about this, pointing out the enormous human misery that was involved in that exchange and that fact that it really hadn't made for an enormously peaceful relationship between Greece and Turkey over the next 75 years, that made no difference to him. He also believed that, and this really fit in the same world view, that Bosnia should be divided with a homogeneous Serb part to the east, and a Croat part - and sometimes it would be different views - either a Croat part that also included the Muslims in the west; and in this context, he looked very much at the idea, for geographic reasons, of exchanging Banja Luka, which was - well, at this point, 1995 - had become almost a purely Serb city as a result of ethnic cleansing - for Tuzla which was an overwhelmingly Muslim city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you hear similar views expressed by other Croatian leaders be with whom you had contact?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Tudjman's views, among the senior Croatian leaders with whom I met, Tudjman's views were pretty much his. He was the one guy who believed in what I call a great Greater Croatia; that is, one that would include the Bosnian Muslims. There were other Croats or Croatians who believed in what I call the smaller Greater Croatia, which would include Herzegovina. This was certainly true of the Defence Minister Gojko Susak, and it's also true of a number of the people in the ruling circles. I would say at that time that 90 per cent or more of the Croatian people actually rejected either idea of Greater Croatia. There was, I think, no support for the idea of dividing Bosnia in two, the way Tudjman wanted to do it. And, on the whole, the Herzegovinians were rather unpopular in Croatia. So while there were sympathy for fellow Croats in Bosnia, there wasn't a strong desire of the Croatian people to annex territory in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 65 of your 92 ter statement, P444, you refer to Mr. Sarinic describing Serbs as a cancer on the stomach of Croatia. Can you describe this for the Court, and what you understood this reflected about his views concerning the continuing presence of Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, once the Serbs had left Croatia, neither Tudjman nor the senior people in his government wanted the Serbs to come back, and Sarinic was in many ways a cipher for Tudjman. Susak and Granic had their own personalities. They would express views that were different from Tudjman, but Sarinic basically repeated what the president wanted. At this time, this is a few weeks after Operation Storm, I am, on instructions from my government, I am criticizing Croatia for the human rights abuses that are taking place in the Krajina, and insisting that as a fundamental matter of human rights, the Serbs should have the right to return home and recover their property. We were also trying to get Croatia to -- to reverse a decision which was to strip the Krajina Serbs of citizenship and to confiscate their property unless they claimed it in 30 days. Of course, nobody was allowed to come back in the 30 days. So this would have been why I was talking to Sarinic about this issue. And in this conversation, in August of 1995, he said, "We cannot except them to come back. They are a cancer in the stomach of Croatia." I just thought that was just a shocking metaphor about people who, we felt, were citizens of the country and had the same rights as other citizens of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me direct your attention next to, and you had begun to do so already, to the period of time after the commencement of Operation Storm and after the majority of Serbs were no longer in the Krajina. In paragraph 42 of your 92 ter statement, you indicate that immediately after the large-scale flight of Serbs from the Krajina, you expressed the view that it was not ethnic cleansing, as explained in testimony during the Milosevic case. Perhaps, it would have been more helpful if the statement included that, your description of that in the Milosevic case or your explanation about that in the Milosevic case. But can you tell the Court what you were referring to by ethnic cleansing in that context, both the context in which you said that and what you meant by saying that it was not ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, ethnic cleansing, as I considered it to be, involved actions to expel the population through military attacks, terror, mass rape, killings, to make sure that everybody who survived left, the burning of homes. Basically, ethnic cleansing was what took place in Croatia in 1991, in Eastern Slavonia, and in the Krajina where the Serbs ethnically cleansed the Croats who lived there, and what took place in Bosnia in 1992 where the Bosnian Serb army used mass killings, mass rape, putting people in concentration camps, destroying their homes, to expel them and to therefore make ethnically pure a large part of Bosnia that had not been Serb but which then became Serb. In my view, the Croatian -- Croatia did not do this in Operation Storm, because when the Croatian forces arrived, the Serbs were already gone. So you couldn't ethnically cleanse somebody who was not there. This is it not to say that they wouldn't have done it had the population been there, but the fact is the population was not there when the Croatian forces actually arrived. So that's what I meant by that statement. I have to say that I, over the years, have regretted that I made it, because it was misunderstood and sort of seemed to be an apology for the Croatian military action, and that was not whey intended. It was simply a technical explanation as to why it was not ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in connection with Serb flight, I also want to ask you about any information you received concerning the role of so-called psy-ops, or psychological operations, or electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, I talked to Defence Minister Susak about this, and he was very proud of the psychological operations in which they had given instructions for -- to the population on how to leave, and a variety of other measures that I have to say at this point some of the details of which escape me. And, of course, I also had reporting from our own sources, for example, the defence attache, about the psychological operations, and then these later became a subject of controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You address that, to some extent, in paragraph 61 of your 92 ter statement, again referring to discussions with Minister Susak, and you say in the third sentence of paragraph 61: "At one point, he said that they had managed to give the order for the Serbian population to leave through their electronic warfare." Did Minister Susak describe the particular order that was given for the Serbian population to leave?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I don't recall that he did. As I recall, he talked about roads that people should take, but my understanding is that the Serbian authorities gave an order for the population to leave. So, as I say in this statement, that he was either from -- he was known to exaggerate, so he may have been taking credit for something that was happening anyhow for an order that the Serbs had given. Incidentally, I should add one another point, which is not in here. The Croatian intelligence on the Serbs was extremely good, and so it is quite possible that the Croatians knew that the Serbs were going to give an order for an evacuation, and then either jump the gun or did things to confuse it as part of their psy-ops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I think that's also reflected in an entry in your diary, which is marked the 9th of August. It is marked on the diary page the 9th of August, which is found at page 38 in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 31 of the e-court version, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's in the second full paragraph. In the bottom of that, you note: "Susak was also very proud of his psy-ops." But I also wanted to ask you about another entry in the diary, and that is Minister Susak saying that one of his planes had bombed a refugee column, but by mistake. I wanted to ask you whether you received information from General Cervenko also concerning attacks on refugee columns, and in that connection -- or prospective attacks on refugee columns. And in that connection, I would like to direct your attention to an entry for the 19th of September, which is at page 57 as marked in the diary, and I believe page 50 in the e-court version. In the second paragraph of the September 19th entry, you refer to a conversation with General Cervenko; and then, after referring to a particular incident, you say: "This is another sign of stress between Cervenko and Susak about which he is remarkably candid. A few weeks ago he showed Clark orders from Susak to open up artillery on 40.000 civilians concentrated in Topusko area because there were ARSK units among them. Cervenko said he went to Tudjman to get that order countermanded."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, interrupt. This matter is outside the scope of this indictment. This is in Sector North.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. As we discussed on a number of other occasions, Your Honour, there is an difference between showing evidence of intent, motive, pattern, and so on, than eliciting evidence specifically designed or directly related to a particular incident for which criminal responsibility is alleged. It is clear that this kind information is relevant and could be useful to the Court in assessing what happened in the indictment area and in the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, Judge, if it was, in fact, relevant, then it should have been in his statement, and it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, concentration of information in statements apparently is the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The statement was taken at a time when I didn't have the diplomatic diary, Your Honour. That document has been disclosed. I believe it has been in the possession of the Defence for some time. In any event, the statements do serve a particular purpose, but they should far from exclusive. There is obviously no intention on the part of the Prosecution, given the timing of receipt of the diplomatic diary, and I might also add that this was contained in the supplemental information sheet at page -- or paragraph -- Again, I may oblige to withdraw that Your Honour. I don't -- I can't find it at the moment. In any event, as I said, we endeavour to put all material available to us in the supplemental information sheet, and the original statements wasn't in possession of the diary at that -- at the time the statement was given. And, furthermore, I mean, it is almost impossible to include all aspects that are relevant to the case in either a 92 ter statement or even supplemental information. So I don't think that is a basis for exclusion. If it became habitual and large portions of evidence that was led from a witness was not available to the Defence, that would be one thing. But in this case, the diary has been available to Mr. Kehoe for at least as long as it has been available to me, if not longer, based on the information received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, how much time you've had to review material that would be - I'm not giving a decision yet - that would be irrelevant, of course, is not a matter that really gives any weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber is aware that this is in evidence, it has been admitted into evidence. The Chamber is not seeking to or would not consider to be greatly assisted by further exploring the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you have already begun to address the issue I next wanted to raised in your discussion concerning Mr. Sarinic's comments. But, as indicated by that testimony, and as in a number of paragraphs in the 92 ter statement, President Tudjman's position on the return of Krajina Serbs was that they simply couldn't come back. Now, you say, in paragraphs 34, 36, and 75 of your statement, that he established constructs to achieve just that. You refer to the 30 days to return or lose property, and then a- and then keeping Serbs from getting back in to meet that condition, the extension to 90 days which was still insufficient. And in paragraph 75, you state that President Tudjman's initial plan was to bar prospective returnees, but that the US forced him to back down. Can you describe, although I know you have begun to do so, these barriers to Serb returns that were erected and how they were implemented and their success?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There were both legal and practical barriers to Serb return. Tudjman referred to these people as "obtansi" [phoen], as people who had opted out of Croatia because they had left. And, initially, in August, Tudjman -- Croatia said that anybody who did not return been 30 days and register for citizenship would not be able to return to Croatia and their property would be confiscated, at which point, then, the confiscated probably would become part of the overall settlement between -- of property claims in the former Yugoslavia, in other words. And, of course, the idea was that Serb property would be offset against Croat property, Croatian property that had been seized or destroyed in Eastern Slavonia and Bosnia and that sort of thing. That was a way to guarantee that people would get absolutely nothing. Under US pressure, the deadline was extended for 90 days in, I suppose, sometime in September. Then it was the -- this deadline was eliminated in sometime in December. And in 1996, again under intense pressure from the United States, Croatia agreed that Serbs could return. But that wasn't the end of the store because, in fact, nobody returned, or almost nobody returned. When the few people did try to return, they found they couldn't get visas if they were in Serbia. If they tried to recover their property, the local officials would never return it. There would be people living in it; nobody would evict those people who were living in it. So, as a practical matter, there were virtually -- the system was set up to guarantee that there would be no returns; and, until 2000, there were virtually no returns or very few. Beyond that, beyond the legal barrier, the effort to legally strip Croatian citizenship from these people, the effort to legally confiscate their property, the Croatian authorities in the Krajina region either ordered or permitted to happen the systematic destruction of -- of all -- of thee greatest part of the Serb important. So once your house was burned and all possessions looted, your farm animals killed or stolen, there was nothing for you to return to. And this, incidentally, was a very marginal part of Croatia, and people had a very low income and suffered from four years of total isolation. People were living at the margin. So when you take away their house, you burn their house, you take away their property, you kill their farm animals, there is no way that anybody can return there and make a living. I believe that was an intentional policy, either orders to destroy the property or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. With regard to that, I object. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, that is the answer the witness gives. He is not asking for beliefs. Of course, there is need to further explore on what his belief is based on, but it's not a reason to intervene. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, either that this was on orders or something that the state authorities permitted to happen because it served their purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you please explore the factual basis on which this one belief or the other belief is based upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, the Court is interested in hearing from you additional information about the basis for your belief that this destruction was intentional; that is, either orders or permitted to happen.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. First, this was when -- this was an area without a population. The people who were there were -- was the Croatian military in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm, so they were in control. This wasn't like the Krajina Serb army or some of the other armed forces. This was the most disciplined military and the best military in the former Yugoslavia, in my view. So there they were, in control; and while they were in control, almost from the start, the looting and burning is taking place. I describe my own observations in Petrinja of going there, I think, on the 6th of August, a few hours after it fell. Again, the Croatian military fully in charge; going back there on the 9th with increasing signs of looting. I had embassy officers down in Knin coming, I think, the 7th or 8th of August - it is in the diary, the precise date - reporting as they were approaching, first through Drnis, seeing recent destruction; coming into Knin where buildings on the outskirts were being burned; one of the officers coming up to some Croatian soldiers and saying, "The house is on fire. Are you going to do anything about it," and then realising that these were the people setting the fires. And, again, given the scale, I don't think that you can argue that these were -- and how long it took or the period of time over which it took place, I don't think that you can say these were isolated incidents. So, to that, I guess I could add a further observation of coming on September 20th to Donji Lapac, a town that was 90 per cent -- 98 per cent Serb, I believe. The most Serb municipality in Croatian in which, in my estimation, 70 per cent of the buildings in Donji Lapac - and these were apartment blocks and things like - had been torched. None much them had been damaged in fighting. They had been systematically torched, and all the ones that hadn't been torched had been all looted. So, again, given the nature of the Croatian state, given that it was a disciplined military, given that it was an organised and efficient state, I don't or I cannot accept the idea that this it was -- that these things happened spontaneously. I can think that they only happened because the Croatian state authorities, Tudjman and his -- the gang around him, wanted this to happen. I put that, then, in the context of Tudjman's desire for an ethnically pure Croatia. His belief in ethnically homogeneous states. I put this in the context of, as we have already discussed, of these laws, the utterly unfair laws, that were intended to prevent, to deny Serbs Croatian citizenship and to confiscate their property. I put this in the context of comments, which I heard from lots of Croatians, that the Serbs were a cancer on -- Krajina Serbs were a cancer on the stomach of Croatia. And, finally, as I look at the transcripts of some of these presidential meetings, you can see, for example, Susak talking, boasting about how Grahovo is now ethnically clean. So these are all the reasons why I believe that either this was on orders or something that was permitted, and I can't say because I don't have a smoking gun of some direct order. But I cannot believe that this happened except for it being something that the Croatian authorities that Tudjman wanted to have happen or was pleased was happening as it was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. On this score, obviously the witness has been shown a series of transcripts from which he bases his opinion, and we would like a list of the transcripts that they -- that the witness was, in fact, actually shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript to which the witness just referred to is the August 12th, which is in evidence. It came in this morning through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With this particular witness, this witness was not a participant in that meeting, but was this witness shown anything else which he wasn't a participant?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the Defence has the full list. I think that we -- that the witness has referred explicitly, to the best of my recollection, to all the transcripts which he was shown, and they've either -- and I think they're in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Here is the problem, Judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Im' sorry to interrupt. This particular issue arises in the context of a presidential transcript which was introduced this morning, and contains a reference which Mr. Kehoe apparently overlooked, but it is in the August 11th transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's not a matter of overlooking that, Judge. What we are entitled to and what General Gotovina is entitled to is the facts and circumstances upon which Ambassador Galbraith is going to testify, be it in his 92 ter statement or a supplemental --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not ask Mr. Galbraith on which transcript he --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I think there is a larger issue here, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that is the issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a separate issue, Judge, which is how are we supposed to prepare to meet, with all due respect, the Ambassador's testimony? How are we supposed to prepare to meet that when such an item of that is not given in the indication, and why was it? Why was it shown to him. This is not something that was a fact that he heard and observed because he was not a part of that meeting. But now we have evidence that it is presented. It is not a fact, it is not something that he observe, certainly a transcript that he reviewed that he was not an participant in, to which we is now have to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I raise just one matter. I'm trying to find an 11th of August transcript, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see minutes of the an August 11th, 1995 meeting, participants. That is P456; that is, 11st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to add to what Mr. Kehoe said. In essence, what is happening here is the Ambassador is being presented with a list of transcript or transcripts most of which he was not a participant in, and then he is asked: "What are your opinions based on the transcripts?" Not directly, but all he is being asked is to give opinion testimony on what the transcripts are, and that's not what the Ambassador is here to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to a misrepresentation what happened. But, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm glad the Court appreciates that. That is precisely my point. First of all, I mean it is a misrepresentation on several levels, first of all, to say most of which he didn't participate in. That was made very clear this morning which documents came in, and I made explicit that this was the only one in which the witness had not participated. I did not seek to elicit testimony from the witness about those transcripts and his conclusions drawn from them. The Defence has been on notice of the witness's views concerning the systematic destruction and the basis for that systematic destruction in the course of a very fulsome answer and very useful answer about how came to that conclusion, the witness appended at the very end his recollection of reading one thing from a transcript which is in evidence. It is extremely unfair and in accurate to accuse the Prosecution of presenting witness with materials so he can form some independent conclusion about it. Beyond that, that, to some extent, that has been something we've seen in other context when documents that witnesses haven't seen have been presented to them, so that they can offer a view about the information contained in those documents based on their own unique experiences in the Krajina. So, even had that been done, it is far from clear there is anything inappropriate about it here, but that's not what happened here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I respond, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we will first see whether there is any need for further debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection. The witness gave some judgements which are always of a mixed nature. We asked or invited Mr. Tieger to further explore the factual basis for that. The witness gave some facts he observed himself; the witness gave some facts that were apparently reported to him, like the soldier who only became aware that it was these soldiers. Mr. Galbraith, I take it you were not standing next to that soldier at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Let me just explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. The exploring the basis on which the witness gave his judgement opens up exactly what sources he used, sources that can be used in cross-examination could explore what he heard or not. Of course, the problem always is that in this kind of situations, that those who participated in meetings matters, et cetera, observed matters, matters are reported to them, they form an opinion on this on which they further act, et cetera. So, therefore, under those circumstances, the objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Might I raise one issue, Your Honour, and it goes exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as it is not challenging the ruling I just gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honour. It's just exploring what Your Honour just said. An Your Honour, at line 23 through 25, exploring exactly what sources he used - I believe you said exactly what sources he used - how do we know what sources he used if we don't have disclosure of those sources? Obviously, it was unknown to us, until just now, that a transcript at which the ambassador was not present was used during the prep session to further whatever testimony the Prosecution was going to lead during the course of this testimony. And absent this one comment about this, it's unknown to me how we are supposed to explore those sources if we do not have disclosure of them. Never, when I was going through this and going through the statements, it didn't dawn on me that something that at which the ambassador was not present, nor participated in, would be used during the course of his prep session, when we were talking and have been talking so much about facts and circumstances. So, unless there is some procedure coming from the Office of the Prosecutor, a disclosure to the Defence of everything that they've shown a witness in preparation, then I think that we don't have any way to explore on cross-examination the sources that he used. The fact of the matter is this particular item was shown to the witness before it went into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you willing to further tell Mr. Kehoe what other material was shown to the witness during the proofing sessions or while preparing his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe, as I stated, that I stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is exactly right. And, furthermore, I think, well, first of all, that's whether or not that's simply an inquiry about matters to or procedures to be adopted in the future, or, in fact, a continuation of the debate about this particular objection is another story. But, there, the Defence has ample opportunity to explore with any witness the basis for his opinions, the documents he was shown, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's the way the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tieger, we are revisiting the same matter. Mr. Kehoe, you heard from Mr. Tieger that the material that was shown to Mr. Galbraith, and, of course, you could ask him whether he has any different recollection, that the matters we have now on our exhibit list and most of which was admitted into evidence that that's the material you went through with the witness in preparing him for his testimony. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. I understand that that's the position with regard to this witness. We have been in trial for sometime, and I don't really know about that, prior witnesses. But I understand with regard to this witness that this is the -- all of the items that have been shown. It does, in fact, present some preparation difficulties as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may please proceed, Mr. Tieger. If there's any reason to revisit this matter in more general terms, then I can tell you Mr. Kehoe whatever documents you get to trace all the impressions, documents, the witness gathers over a couple of years being, I would say, involved in many matters to - of course, it is fair that we have it now on or list what was shown to the witness - but to have the illusion that you could find the roots of every tiny little bit of that is just impossible. Let's be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Judge, and I know that the Ambassador's long experience in this area and his positions have been formulated by many different facts and circumstances. I'm concerned about is the documents that are shown to witnesses before they come into this courtroom. Now it did surprise me that this, in fact, has been shown to this witness and has been used as a basis, further basis, of his position. And that's what I'm concerned with, not everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Mr. Tieger you, may proceed. While I'm looking at the clock, perhaps it is even wiser to have a break. I have to apologise. During the last break, I was doing something else and just forgot about the time, which I do not encourage anyone to do. I will try to improve my performance and back at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I heard that you would like to put something on the record in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What I'd like to address with the Court is the fact that this witness is, in fact, giving what is essentially expert testimony based on his opinion. Obviously, there has been no notice of that score under Rule 94 bis. But, in essence, the testimony that he has given for the past, well, some time, in this session, has not been based on facts -- excuse me, has been based on facts, but then he opines on those and offers his conclusion. That is expert testimony; and based on that we object to that testimony because, number one, he has not been noted as an expert and such testimony is violation of Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your objection is on the record and gives the Chamber, at this moment, no reason to not further receive the witness of this witness. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the parties, I do not know whether I misspoke on 67, line 25. I think I said to receive the evidence of the witness; whereas, the transcript says otherwise. I do not know whether I made the mistake or whether the mistake was made by another. If I did it, apologies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, can we next call up P446.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to direct your attention to P446 which is a coded cable, and I believe is dated 31 August 1995. Just for the benefit of the Chamber, in deciphering some aspects of the cables, is it correct that you can identify the date of that document by the notation which is immediately to the left of the unclassified marking at the top?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it indicates the month and the year to the right, and then the date is the first notation of the --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: And the time. So it would be the 31st of August -- I'm sorry, even with these glasses. I think it is 11.15 -- sorry. Well, it's 1518, Zulu.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. If this is helpful, it is contained in tab 5 of your binder. It might make it easier to read.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you described, earlier in your testimony, the views about a largely ethnically homogeneous Croatia and the constructs implemented to keep Serbs from returning. I want to ask you if you were aware of who was supposed -- what Croatian leaders intended for the demi-graphics of the Krajina in the aftermath of Operation Storm. And I want to turn your attention to paragraph 43 of P446 which indicates as follows: "The offensive and resultant population displacements has caused a massive refugee problem. The Croatian public announcement to give security guarantees to the Serbs in the region was intended for Western propaganda purposes. The goal of the Croatians is to 'ethnic cleanse' the region to make room for approximately," and the coma looks like 100.000, but there appears to be an extra zero. Perhaps you will be able to clarify. "Croatian refugees to settle in the area," and then it goes on to describe how that is substantiated by the practice of taking Serbs to transition camps. First of all, Ambassador, was that your understanding at the time; that is, that the goal was to make room for Croatian refugees in lieu of the Krajina Serbs who had fled?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The first point I would make is that Tudjman, when really pressed, spoke about, you know, maybe 10 percent of the Serb population being there; although, though I think he was against any of it being there. That, of course, left a lot of vacant space, and his idea was that Croats from the Diaspora might then come to the Krajina and settle there. It is possible that he spoke or the Croatian leadership spoke about 100.000 Croat refugees from the fighting in Bosnia. That would be some from Eastern Slavonia. Also, he expected some people to come back from the Diaspora, and that they would all come and settle there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could turn your attention next to P447, that's in tab 6 of your binder, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a coded cable dated 11 December 1995, and is this a cable from you, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is a cable from me, and it is a cable that I personally wrote, which is evident from the use of the first person. Also, it was sent in a channel that would have gone directly to the Secretary of State. It was sent, I believe, in anticipation of his visit to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment. Now, Ambassador, this cable indicates that, in paragraph 3: "Croatia continued to bar Krajina Serbs from returning their homes and has arbitrarily confiscated their property. Far from being apologetic, Tudjman yesterday told visiting congressman that it would be impossible for these Serbs to return to the place where their families lived for centuries. The burning of Sipovo, for which he rightly called Tudjman on the carpet, was part of a broader strategy to creat a Serb-free cordon sanitaire around the Croatian heartland. The same systematic burnings of Serb homes followed Croatia's August capture of Krajina and September capture of Serb towns in western Bosnia. None of this was," as Tudjman claimed to you, "the isolated acts of angry men." Can you describe to the Court what you were intending to convey with this cable, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was intending to convey the same thing that I did in the answer I gave before the break, which is that - these were judgements that I formed in 1995, as is obvious from this cable that - that the systematic destruction of the Krajina was something that was either planned or permitted, but anyhow it was something that was intended to happen by the Croatian -- by Tudjman and the Croatian authorities. It was not because or it didn't take place because of angry Croats returning and wanting to take revenge on Serb property. It wasn't isolated acts. It was a matter of state policy. That was my message to the Secretary Of State, and that was a judgement that I formed well before I sent this cable because it is reflected in other messages I sent as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Had you sent a similar message -- I'm violating the rule of pausing. Had you sent a similar message to the secretary earlier in the year?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: On September 11th -- I should explain, for the benefit of the Court, there is an channel in which an ambassador sends a message directly to the Secretary of State, either it can be very sensitive issues, but usually on policy -- or quite often it would be on policy matters, and it isn't used very frequently. But on September 11th, I sent a cable exactly on this subject, in which I again said that what was going -- the destruction in the Krajina was part of a pattern intended to make it impossible for Serbs to return home, and that the United States should condition its relations with Croatian on Croatia permitting Serbs to return home, giving them citizenship on their permitting Serbs to recover their property, making restitution for property that was destroyed, on providing conditions of security so that people could return home. And if Croatia didn't do that, we should have a series of really very strong measures that we would not -- we would block Croatia's integration into Western structures and talk to our European allies of keeping them out of the European structures, that we would keep them out of the NATO structures, that unless Croatia did these things, we would not be supportive of the reintegration of Eastern Slavonia. In other words, that our entire relationship should depend significantly on Croatia's reversal of a policy that was in place, which was to prevent the return of Serbs and to, by law, and by -- by having conditions of insecurity in the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, you refer in this cable to a Serb-free cordon sanitaire around the Croatian heartland. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. In the area to the west of -- of the Krajina region in Bosnia which had been Serb-populated, Croatia had taken this over in the 1995 offensive that followed Storm, and allowed or ordered the systematic burning of Serbs' homes and properties, preventing Serbs from returning to this area. The idea was that this thing would become a Croatian area, it would be a buffer to Croatia proper, and I think it was also part of Tudjman's idea that this area would along with Herzegovina eventually be annexed to Croatia as part of this scheme of a Greater Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you -- I'm going to refer to paragraph 23 of P445, and ask you if you saw personally examples of what you just referred to and also heard and also received reports about it.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for benefit of the Court, if I could call up the P52 -- or, excuse me, 65 ter 5233.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's, I believe, tab 17 in your binder, Ambassador. It takes time because maps take a long time to load electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you are aware that there was a possible objection against this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think earlier we discussed the adding this -- this map to the 65 ter list, and I then reserved the position of the Chamber as far as relevance is concerned for this map. So, perhaps, also in your questions make it immediately clear what the relevance is; and then before the witness answer the question, then at least the Defence should have an opportunity to oppose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, you refer, in paragraph 23 of your supplemental information sheet, to observing what happened when the HVO took over some towns in western Bosnia and seeing it in several places, including Mrkonjic Grad. Can you first point out where Mrkonjic Grad is on this map?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is in western Bosnia; I guess, to be precise, the north-west quadrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could enlarge that, yeah, the portion of the map to the left. Sorry. Okay. And if the cursor could be moved to the right. All right. A little further to the right, please. A little further to the left. I'm sorry. I think the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, perhaps you can direct the -- are you referring to the right, to the area where the cursor is now shown?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: And you will note is Sipovo is just below there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then referring to the cordon sanitaire that you testified about, is -- does that include the area shown in red on the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection at this point, of course, relevance on this particular. The other aspect of this particular aspect is if this is some allegation with regard to the HV, this was not HV-controlled territory. At any point, it was controlled by the ABiH, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no need to belabour the point. The witness referred to certain locations. I indicated I thought it would be helpful to the Court to observe those locations. I tendered the map, but I don't need to go into it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The problem is, number one, obviously our initial objection concerning going into these Bosnian matters; but, number two, this was an area that was not under HV control, nor is there in any foundation that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I mean, you are apparently formulating your objection on the basis of an assumption; that is, what I did not hear in the question of Mr. Tieger that this was an area under HV control. The witness referred to a certain place. Mr. Tieger now asked where we find this on the map. So I'm colour-blind for this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if I can just clarify, what I am saying is that at this town was, in fact, burned, it was not under HV control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're giving evidence, Mr. Kehoe, which we leave usually to the witnesses. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's fine. I would also add that there has been testimony in this case earlier, and with this witness, concerning Grahovo and Glamac. I think, to the extent that the ethnic composition of those locations is of assistance to the Court, I think, the map is useful in that regard as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, of course, the source, I don't know whether it is a contested source, but it appears to be an ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We're just focussing only on the border areas there, and this is a map which is based on or depicts the results of the 1991 census. Is there any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with this particular map, if it is the census map of the typical census map, no, I don't have a dispute about that. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's at least now clear. Is there any dispute about whether the map does reflect properly the outcome of the census? We have not yet heard or the only thing that is said until now, and there Mr. Tieger was more or less giving evidence which I think he should leave to others, is that Mr. Tieger said Grahovo and Glamac. I think that you added something like that this was mainly Serb areas, but I can't find it on the transcript, so I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... this is in reference to the map itself, Your Honour. What the map depicts about the demographics of that area is linked to earlier testimony concerning those areas. That's all, and it could be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just trying to determine the extent to which I may be able to curtail the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Quick question, Ambassador: In paragraphs 46 of your statement, at 46 at 56, you refer to criticism by the United States and by you of the crimes that were taking place and the responses of Croatian officials. You indicate, in particular in paragraph 56, that you were constantly raising the issue of atrocities with various leaders and what response you received. In paragraph 13 of your supplemental information sheet, that's P445, you refer to a response from Foreign Minister Granic who told you on 13 October that he had not defended Croatia's conduct after Storm because he couldn't do that. He disapproved of what was happening in the Krajina, and wanted to make sure that you understood and didn't associate him with it. I wanted to ask you if that 13 October discussion with Mr. Granic is also reflected in your diary of that date?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, just to round this out a bit, after the -- after Operation Storm and the events that you described in the weeks and months that followed the commencement of Operation Storm, did you continue to engage in efforts to resolve the conflict in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was the principal mediator, along with UN Envoy Thorvald Stoltenberg, the editor of the Erdut Agreement, which provided for the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, the last bit of Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Erdut Agreement, that was concluded when?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: November 12th 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you go on to engage in efforts in Dayton to resolve the overall conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I had been at Dayton at the very beginning and at the very end; but for most of the Dayton period, I was, in fact, working on doing shuttle diplomacy between Zagreb and Erdut, which is where the local Serbs met to try and resolve that problem. The Dayton talks began on the 1st of November, so this was something that occurred simultaneously with Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did the Erdut Agreement signal the beginning of the end of the conflict in Croatia between Croatian and the Krajina Serbs, or was there continued fighting thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No. It very much was the beginning of the end, and I have to say what it provided for was a two-year UN transitional administration which Croatian authority was gradually introduced, and at the time end of that two-year period, most of the Serb population remained. Some part of the Croat population which had been expelled in 1991 returned, but it was the first time in that five-year period, four-year period that a territory changed hands and the population that was not from the group that was acquiring the territory actually remained. I might also add that one of -- this was very much related to our concerns about the fate of the other Serbs in Croatia, because in order to get this peace agreement in Slavonia, we had to persuade the Eastern Slavonian Serbs that they could live in Croatia and be full citizens of the country. That was very hard to do when there were laws that said if you didn't return in 30 days, you would lose your property. And, furthermore, some part of the Serbs from the Krajina had gone to Eastern Slavonia. So the question was how would you handle them. We needed to have a Croatia that followed international standards for human rights, which meant people who were citizens of that country had a right to the citizenship and had the right to the property. That was essential, not just because it was right, not just because it an internationally recognised human rights, but because it was essential to the peace process in Easter Slavonia; and Eastern Slavonia was, in fact, essential to getting to the Dayton Peace Agreement. So there was a lot of stake on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just have a moment. Your Honour, that concludes my examination-in-chief, and I would tender the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, I will also indicate to my learned friends that I will had some bar table submissions. utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have seven day period of tome just to look at them. They're quite extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.text: They are extensive in that respect, and I don't have any theoretical problem with the time-period. I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't insist on an immediate decision; that would not be fair. And, again, I'm just trying to balance the Court's interest in having the documents available at the earlier opportunity, against the Defence need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no. If there would be any objections, I take it that the Chamber would need to have them available anyhow, because we would then have to look at the documents in order to decide on the objections. So, therefore, the Chamber would like to receive whatever the position of the Defence will be already to receive those, those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would only add, Your Honour, to the extent is Defence is aware of any objections to those documents, that it might implicate, if not the need, then the utility of raising them with this witness, then we would certainly like to know as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that is it understood, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, while they're discussing, we got the e-mail on the 20th and I got the two binders worth of documents during the break, so it is going take a little bit of time.

utterances.text: Yes. The invitation is that whenever something comes into your mind, don't hesitate to already inform Mr. Tieger and the Chamber about any objections. utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Misetic highlights to me that the one issue that comes up is the 8th -- August 3rd transcript [sic], which involves the ambassador. We don't have an objection to that. We will be putting the audio in during the course of the testimony, so I don't believe that with the array that the Prosecution just put in that that is the only one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is the 8th --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the 3rd, Your Honour. It's the 3rd of August.

utterances.text: P448, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P448. Then, Mr, Kehoe, you will be the first one to cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
