utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, you will be first cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador, good to see you again.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would like to talk to you, if we could just go back to your 92 ter statement. I believe it is 444. I would like to go back to some of your discussions about the Krajina Serbs, and just predate your discussions with Mr. Babic in Belgrade, and just go back a bit further and ask you to elaborate on a few matters, if you could. And I'd like to direct your attention, first, to paragraph 6 of your 92 ter statement, and you note that Slobodan Milosevic called all the shots with the Krajina Serbs: "Among other things, including what I saw of his control at negotiations, Milosevic was involved with the payment of salaries of the ARSK and possibly police. All the fuel came from Serbia and was obvious that the Krajina Serbs were heavily dependant on Serbia." Just waiting for the translation to catch up. Mr. Ambassador, tell us a little bit about the control that Slobodan Milosevic exercised over the Krajina Serbs, if you could?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was very substantial. He manipulated the elections in the Krajina in 1994 to defeat Babic and to bring Martic into power. He paid the salaries, he supplied the fuel. I believe or I'm sure that he was the one who obstructed the Z-4 plan, for reasons that had little to do with Krajina, but with his concerns about Kosovo and his hope to make some deal with Tudjman, who frankly was open to a deal, in which Serbia might acquire some Croatian territory. So, yeah, I think he very much called the shots in the Krajina. I could go on at greater length, but that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me -- just following up on your statement, did he control the military as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes, he certainly did. He changed the general after the -- after rockets were sent on to Zagreb, on May 2nd and 3rd of 1995, I think in part because he didn't want to have another rocket attack on Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would have been the replacement of General Celeketic by of General Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When the Krajina Serbs were initially set up back in 1991, was he receiving the report of Slobodan Milosevic as far as back as then?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe -- that I believe is the case. Obviously, I only came on the scene full time in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ambassador. And you noted for us that you believe that he rigged the election, if you will, in 1994. Can you tell us about that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Babic was, I think, the most popular person in the Krajina, and I think he was the one leader who had some, and I want to underscore the word "some," real concern for the population. And, therefore, he had some degree of independence from Milosevic, and Milosevic didn't like that. So you had a vote, and, again, you have to go back and check the records. I'm doing this from memory, but it was quite extra ordinary. In the first round, I think Martic got 24 per cent and Babic got 48 or 49 per cent, and somehow in the second round Martic actually won. I think you would have to -- this is almost unprecedented in the history of run-offs, that you have that kind of switch from one round to the next, where all the votes go to the candidate who finished second when he was that far behind. Again, you would have to check on the exact percentages. I may not have it right, but I think I have it right in the generality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So your conclusion, at the time, was that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So your conclusion at the time that even through 1995, he was directing matters in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just backing up to 1991, and I'd like to ask you just a couple of questions about the Greater Serbia and Milosevic's involvement in some of that, and I just reference some of your prior testimony. We are not going to go into it in great detail. But in this testimony that you gave in the Milosevic case at page 23081 that you said, at line 21, that you believe that Slobodan Milosevic was the architect of a policy of creating a Greater Serbia and that little happened without his knowledge or involvement. Can you explain that for us a little bit?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, there are many aspects of this: One is that the JNA, which was the Yugoslav People's Army, was responsible to -- Milosevic was effectively in charge of it; and, nominally, it was a different structure. And the JNA - and this was, of course, when the Krajina rebellion began; this was part of Yugoslavia, at least legally - the JNA did not behave as a neutral force, but it sided with the Krajina Serbs, helping to cease this area from Croatia. Then in Bosnia, in 1992, it was even more blatant. Milosevic and the JNA arranged for the Bosnian Serbs in the JNA to be in Bosnia; and then at one point in time, something like May of 1992, the JNA withdrew from -- from Bosnia. I think, maybe, at that point, it was renamed the Yugoslav People's Army. What remained in Bosnia, which was JNA with all the equipment, with all the logistics, became the Bosnian Serb army. And I could also go on to add, as we did the peace negotiations in Dayton, the man who we negotiated with was Milosevic, even though these were peace negotiations about -- that theoretically was about the sovereign state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and where the Bosnian Serb leaders were present. Basically we didn't talk to them at all. The -- e got the deal by talking to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So he spoke for every -- for all the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So was it clear to you, Mr. Ambassador, that when the Krajina Serbs had set up their rebel government, it was the idea of ultimately becoming part of this Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. That is my belief, at the time that it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a map, if I may, and this is it 1D33-0001. I'm sorry, can we make that 1D33-0002. Let's take look at this initially, if we could just examine this and if we could move to the next map, which is a little bit more specific, 1D33-0002. Mr. Ambassador, this is a map that was the borders of the Greater Serbia, according to the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. Mr. Ambassador, was that your understanding of what the aspirations of the Greater Serbia advocates, including Slobodan Milosevic for their ultimate goal of achieving a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I don't know if this particular map reflected those aspirations. I testified that Tudjman was a very strategic thinker. You may not like his strategy but he was very strategic. Milosevic, in my view, was not strategic at all, he was very tactical, and he eventually manoeuvred Serbia down to the size it is today. So whether at some point he had this in mind, or people around him, what -- his goals kept changing because, again, I don't think he really thought strategically, but he did want a Greater Serbia. Some of this territory, obviously Split would seem to me to have been a -- and perhaps some of the territory in Slovenia would have been going too far. But he certainly wanted a Greater Serbia that included a fair amount of what is shown on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could continue on, and let's get down to the effect of the breakaway republic -- the so-called Republic of Serb Krajina. Did it in fact divide Croatia into several parts? And, if so, what did it do to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, the first point is that it divided, if you will, mainland Croatia from the coast. When I -- when I took up my responsibilities as ambassador, there was in fact no land link between Split, which was Croatia's second city, and Zagreb, which was its largest city and capital, and that is because the Serb territory came down to an inlet by Maslenica, and there wasn't a bridge there. Shortly after I arrived, a bridge was built and the Serbs shelled it. But in June of 1993, the country was divided. The way people had to travel was either by boat, which is what I did on my first trip to Split, or you took a ferry over to the island of Pag and you bypassed this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this particular situation was going on from 1991 certainly until the 1995 period of time, by and large, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It got -- the answer, by and large, yes; but it did get better in 1993 with the opening of the Maslenica bridge, and it got better, significantly better, I think, in 1994 after the cease-fire, which was the first stage of the Z-4 process, the cease-fire of 29 March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's a practical matter -- I'm sorry, I got to take break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. It is a quarter to 2.00. Perhaps we first ask the witness, Mr. Galbraith, I should like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony -- the testimony you have already given today or the testimony still to be given in the days to come. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, and if I'm not mistaken, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the calender had us tomorrow afternoon, in Courtroom II, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm not wrong on one front but on both, Mr. Kehoe, that must be some conciliation to you. Mr. Galbraith, we would like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.00 and in Courtroom III, as you -- no, II, Courtroom II - now I am really making all the mistakes I can make - which is a far smaller courtroom. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Galbraith out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour. I just wanted to call your attention to a scheduling issue. I don't know how long this is going to last, and I am afraid I had assumed it was all morning sessions. But I have to back with my children who are in Norway on Thursday evening because my wife is leaving the next morning and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, one of the things why I asked Mr. Usher to escort you out of the courtroom because that's what -- exactly what I wanted to raise with the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be informed as soon as possible, although the unexpected now and then happens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that. Just if there is afternoon sessions, it becomes harder, on Thursday. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, one short question to you. The Chamber wondered whether what we heard over the last 15 minutes, whether when we're talking about Greater Serbia, when we are talking about a lot of other things, whether that was contested by the Defence, the role of -- most part of the role of Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nothing that I heard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one. Mr. Kehoe, you raised the issue of relevance, time-frame, territorial scope several times. Now we find ourselves in a situation where you apparently have sought to elicit evidence from this witness which is not contested in any way, certainly is mainly outside the scope, the temporal scope of the indictment, and the geographical scope as well. As I said before, background is background and should not become foreground. So I'm not saying that you could not touch upon these issues but, first of all, it would perhaps have been good to verify with Mr. Tieger to what extent there is any major difference of view on -- on the Greater Serbia idea, and it could of course mean that in the follow-up that we get to the real core. But when assessing how the time in cross-examination was used, either at the end of the day tomorrow, or the day after that, the Chamber certainly will take into consideration whether you started focussing on the most vital points or whether we spent lots of time on background rather on that what really is in the foreground of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. First, Your Honour, I was up for 15 minutes and getting into this area, and this area was brought to the fore, which we will develop, because it is quite clear that based on the testimony that was elicited from this witness vis-a-vis Mr. Babic and those negotiations in the first couple of day the of August of 1995, that the Prosecution is trying to challenge the necessity for launching Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Tieger? One necessity -- I always thought that, as such, the military operation as such whether there would have been other ways out, that that is not the issue in this case, whether it was justified or not justified to regain Croatian territory. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That position, Your Honour, as discussed earlier, has not changed. Nevertheless, it is relevant and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so whether it was necessary or relevant, I mean, I do understand that that is not the issue, although the witness has spent a few words, a few lines on -- in his statement, to some extent a bit repetitiously, introduced again today that there might have been other options still available at the 2nd or 3rd or 4th of August. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it was not a subject of debate, why was it led in direct examination? Your Honour has been on the parties about taking unnecessary issues that aren't on the table, and we spent 45 minutes talking about his negotiations with Babic and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's a fair reflection of what happened. The -- as I said before, background should be background. It could well be, Mr. Kehoe, and therefore I'm expressing myself in a cautious way, that where we have now the background that we get quickly to the foreground. Nevertheless I would say that you were rather far away from the conflict. At least Mr. Tieger stayed within the year mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, two years, Judge, 199e and 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He could not change the date of appointment of Mr. -- Ambassador Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing that I would like to convey to you is that it's the shared view of this Chamber that there is at least a risk that you run out of time where the background has been fully illuminated and the foreground not yet, and it's just for you to be aware that this is the provisional impression of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with all due respect, I have to take issue with that, given the fact that the Chamber didn't stop the Prosecution from going through an issue that they now say was not a subject of debate, and that my issue, and given the fact that he was going to go through that, was simply trying to answer that issue. That's how I started with the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm not seeking, as a matter of fact to have a full debate on this at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, Your Honour. My response was in connection with matters raised earlier; that is, the legal justification for launching Operation Storm and whether that is at issue in this case. The intent behind is it another matter, and to the extent that the information provided can be useful to the Court in assessing the circumstances and to the extent that there was any imminent prospect of peace and that was known to various people within the region, I think the Court has already seen evidence from witnesses, regular witnesses who were aware of that, it sheds light on all of that. It is useful in -- in that way. Now, this is a different story from whether or not the Prosecution contests Slobodan Milosevic's role in the Krajina, and if -- to the extent that the Court inquired about the Prosecution's position in connection with that, I think all parties are aware of that, in view of the cases that have preceded this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I see quite some differences between starting with the Greater Serbia issue or whether we focus on what happened in the last days before Storm and the context in which, for example, the issue, which apparently is a contested issue, who invited or urged the Serb population to leave, or whether they were at all urged to leave, and, if so, by whom, that appears to be all within the last couple of day, weeks, months, perhaps. Mr. Kehoe, I do see that you do not agree with me. The main issue I wanted to raise is that if we're running out of time, that the Chamber, on the basis of the observations, until now, sees that this is a risk, and you have now convinced me there is only a small risk of not having heard the foreground and have spent too much time on the background. We're not going to discuss this at this moment any further. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry I didn't want to interrupt, I know we're running out of time. I wanted to raise this issue before we adjourned and that is I see from the schedule that we are currently expected to have an afternoon session on Thursday. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it can -- if that can be changed. If we needed all the Thursday afternoon session. Could I then inquire, and then I really stop, on how much time the Defence teams would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm going to play the audios of the transcripts that you heard, and -- in part. That will take some time to go through this and the various nuances that have been laid out. This is a very, very extensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you start with the explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I want Your Honour to understand because I don't seem to be doing well the other way. When I give you a time-frame without giving an idea of where I'm going, I don't seem to be very successful, so I would like to tell exactly where I'm going, and as I will tell you where I'm going on this Greater Serbia issue, but I would say with what I am doing here will take me about six hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I do ask any questions, it wouldn't be more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then for the Markac Defence. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously it depends on what happens before me, but two hours at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours at least. We will consider it and have a look at Thursday's session. We stand adjourned until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of June, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
